messages.subject: Feature Request - Segments for Individual Samples and Plotting
messages.subject_clean: Feature Request - Segments for Individual Samples and Plotting
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I have been checking out the latest Sequenza code on BitBucket, and have been utilizing the new $depths element that provides depths to mean / median ratios for the individual samples used (both raw and normalized). They have been very useful!

I was wondering if you might implement a couple additional features: 1) perform segmentation on at least the normalized depths (both samples); and 2) include that in the RData extract; optional: 3) plot the segments in red in the new chromosome depths PDF.

Thanks,
Erich

messages.subject: Re: chromosome seems to be removed when I run sequenza.extract
messages.subject_clean: chromosome seems to be removed when I run sequenza.extract
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

it can be that the sorting of the chromosomes of the 2 mpileups and the GC window file are not compatible. This may result in a seqz file that have only fewer chromosomes (depending on the overlaps of the chromosomes during the parsing of the 3 files).

To overcome the issue, you could manually generate seqz files for each chromosome and then merge the various files afterwards.

If you are interested, I also developed a general workflow framework (it’s just a python library) that implements a sequenza pipeline. It generates the seqz files for each chromosome and merge the resulting files in a unique seqz file, so it should bypass your current problem. If you think this would be useful I can expand on that...

Francesco

messages.body_plain:
Hi Erich,

thanks for the feedback! Yes, I think that splitting the depths is quite useful, also for QC purpose.
I can try to implement the segmentation on individual samples, although that should increase considerably the running time.
The segmentation should be performed with a depth only approach (rather then an allele specific approach), this is by far slower then the default segmentation algorithm used in the extract function.

But I agree, that would be very useful (eg to exclude regions with germline CNV - or just messy regions in the normal -).
If I manage to include the segmentation (point 1), there is no reason not to include point 2 and 3.
Maybe I can add a flag in the sequenza.extract interface that triggers the segmentation of the samples when enabled. So the user expects a slower running with the option, rather then be slow by default…

Francesco

messages.subject_clean: chromosome seems to be removed when I run sequenza.extract
messages.body_plain:
Hi.

There are some problems when I ran 'sequenza-utils.py pileup2seqz' since the size of out.seqz.gz file was smaller than others.
So I could solve the problem by re run pileup2seqz.:)
Still, really thank you for your kindly answering.

Can I ask you one more thing?

when sequenza finds the copy number of A allele and B allele, does it consider the neighbor SNVs of mutations?

I would like to know the mutations were appeared after amplification of alleles or not.
But It seems to difficult to know it with outputs of sequenza.

for example, when the number of mutation is 1, the copy number of A allele is 2, and B allele is 1.
There can be two possible interpretation.

one is AA' B  => mutation was in A allele and occured after amplification of A allele.
second is AA B' => mutation was occured in B allele, and B was not amplified.

Can I know which interpretation was right with the outputs of sequenza?
If sequenza considered the SNVs, I thought I could know by comparing SNVs of normal and tumor of that position which has mutation.

Thank you.
Bin.

messages.subject: Re: sequenza.extract error
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I’ve seen you also opened an issue about the parallel processing.
I think it’s possible, however it may be too convoluted to include the support in the package.

Basically, you could easily run sequenza.extract for a single chromosome in parallel, then run for each object sequenza.fit, separately.
Each sequenza.fit instance will give a separate CP object
The CP object, is a list with the info:
    ploidy: A numeric vector of tested ploidy values
    cellularity: A numeric vector of tested cellularity values
    lpp: Anumeric matrix of log-posterior probability for each (ploidy, cellularity) pair.

Be aware that sequenza.fit may fail if there are no segments to feed the model, so you may setup some error checking try() to fallback to a default CP object, with all 0s in the lpp matrix (or some other approach you may end up with).

The lpp of all the resulting CP objects can be sum to get the “final” CP object, which would equivalent to the CP object as you had run the program sequentially.

It may be a little overhead, but it should work :). I’m not expert on how to parallelize this, I would do something like:

> library(sequenza)
> library(parallel)
>
> data.file <- system.file("data", "example.seqz.txt.gz",
>     package = "sequenza")
>
> chromosome <- c(1:22, c("X", "Y"))
>
> n_cpu = 4 # or any other amount of parallel processes you want
>
> sample_stats <- gc.sample.stats(data.file)
>
> extract_chroms <- mclapply(chromosome, FUN = function(x, seqz_file, gc_stats) {
>         sequenza.extract(seqz_file, chromosome.list = x, gc.stats= gc_stats)
>     },
>     seqz_file = data.file, gc_stats = sample_stats, mc.cores = n_cpu)
>
>
> CP_chroms <- mclapply(extract_chroms, FUN = function(x) {
>  sequenza.fit(x, mc.cores = 1) # adjust mc.cores, beware that each process
>                                # will try to use the number of cpu you set
>                                # here so it will fork exponentially
> }, mc.cores = n_cpu)
>
> CP_chroms_lpp <- sapply(1:length(CP_chroms), FUN = function(x, y) y[[x]]["lpp"], y = CP_chroms)
> CP_chroms_lpp[is.na <http://is.na>(CP_chroms_lpp)] <- NULL
> CP_lpp <- Reduce("+", CP_chroms_lpp)
>
> CP <- list(cellularity = CP_chroms[[1]]$cellularity, ploidy = CP_chroms[[1]]$ploidy, lpp = CP_lpp)
> cp.plot(CP)
> cp.plot.contours(CP, add = T)
>
> res <- get.ci <http://get.ci>(CP)
>
> res$max.cellularity
>
> res$max.ploidy
>

Francesco

> On Thu, Aug 31, 2017 at 9:23 AM, Francesco Favero <favero.f...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I’ve seen you also opened an issue about the parallel processing.
> > I think it’s possible, however it may be too convoluted to include the support in the package.
> >
> > Basically, you could easily run sequenza.extract for a single chromosome in parallel, then run for each object sequenza.fit, separately.
> > Each sequenza.fit instance will give a separate CP object
> > The CP object, is a list with the info:
> >     ploidy: A numeric vector of tested ploidy values
> >     cellularity: A numeric vector of tested cellularity values
> >     lpp: Anumeric matrix of log-posterior probability for each (ploidy, cellularity) pair.
> >
> > Be aware that sequenza.fit may fail if there are no segments to feed the model, so you may setup some error checking try() to fallback to a default CP object, with all 0s in the lpp matrix (or some other approach you may end up with).
> >
> >
> > The lpp of all the resulting CP objects can be sum to get the “final” CP object, which would equivalent to the CP object as you had run the program sequentially.
> >
> > It may be a little overhead, but it should work :). I’m not expert on how to parallelize this, I would do something like:
> >
> > > library(sequenza)
> > > library(parallel)
> > >
> > > data.file <- system.file("data", "example.seqz.txt.gz",
> > >     package = "sequenza")
> > >
> > > chromosome <- c(1:22, c("X", "Y"))
> > >
> > > n_cpu = 4 # or any other amount of parallel processes you want
> > >
> > > sample_stats <- gc.sample.stats(data.file)
> > >
> > > extract_chroms <- mclapply(chromosome, FUN = function(x, seqz_file, gc_stats) {
> > >         sequenza.extract(seqz_file, chromosome.list = x, gc.stats= gc_stats)
> > >     },
> > >     seqz_file = data.file, gc_stats = sample_stats, mc.cores = n_cpu)
> > >
> > >
> > > CP_chroms <- mclapply(extract_chroms, FUN = function(x) {
> > >  sequenza.fit(x, mc.cores = 1) # adjust mc.cores, beware that each process
> > >                                # will try to use the number of cpu you set
> > >                                # here so it will fork exponentially
> > > }, mc.cores = n_cpu)
> > >
> > > CP_chroms_lpp <- sapply(1:length(CP_chroms), FUN = function(x, y) y[[x]]["lpp"], y = CP_chroms)
> > > CP_chroms_lpp[is.na <http://is.na/>(CP_chroms_lpp)] <- NULL
> > > CP_lpp <- Reduce("+", CP_chroms_lpp)
> > >
> > > CP <- list(cellularity = CP_chroms[[1]]$cellularity, ploidy = CP_chroms[[1]]$ploidy, lpp = CP_lpp)
> > > cp.plot(CP)
> > > cp.plot.contours(CP, add = T)
> > >
> > > res <- get.ci <http://get.ci/>(CP)
> > >
> > > res$max.cellularity
> > >
> > > res$max.ploidy
> > >
